title: ‘I Didn’t Really Sleep’: Inside the Investigation That Helped End Viktor Orbán’s Rule
content:
On April 12, Hungary went to the polls. The result was a landslide win for Péter Magyar and the Tisza party, and the end of 16 years of rule by Viktor Orbán and his “illiberal democracy.”

Just three weeks before, Hungarian investigative newsroom and GIJN member Direkt36, in partnership with Telex, broke the story of a secret operation to bring down Tisza — and secret service efforts to sabotage the police investigation into the operation.

“Neither the article nor the interview was a routine journalistic job,” Direkt36 founder and editor András Petho shared in a LinkedIn post. “They were the results of a months-long, complex investigation that we conducted under immense pressure and at high risk.” The story, he adds, was one of the biggest scandals of the election, “if not the whole Orbàn era.”

Direkt36 obtained documents from a source and spoke with multiple whistleblowers familiar with Tisza’s internal affairs — including a former volunteer for the party, a man responsible for protecting its internal systems, and a police officer familiar with the investigation — to confirm details of a secret operation to bring down the party’s IT systems and hack into party databases.

creator: Laura Oliver

title: Global Data Center Energy Use, US Strike on Iran School, Russia’s Security Service Leaks, Portugal’s Ancient Trees
content:
An investigation by the Sky News data and forensics team suggests that the US likely used outdated intelligence to strike an Iranian school with Tomahawk missiles in February, killing 156 people, most of them children, despite years of internal warnings about out-of-date targeting information. Our Top 10 in Data Journalism round-up, looking at stories from July 8 to 22, also includes an IStories investigation into the surveillance priorities of a section of Russia’s “second service” police force, a cross-border investigation led by Lighthouse Reports on how big food companies used lawsuits and legal threats to block public health efforts, and the South China Morning Post’s deep dive into Hong Kong’s aging population.

title: How to Make Investigations Matter More: A Q&A with the Authors of ‘The Guide to Impact Journalism’
content:
In recent years, the term “impact” has been used a lot in journalism, the NGO sector, and beyond. In investigative journalism, many newsrooms have begun implementing an “impact strategy.” But how can they do better, what is the goal, and on what practices should they rely?

It was while seeking answers to these questions for their own needs that the investigative media outlet Disclose, a member of GIJN, and the independent media outlet Rembobine published “The Guide to Impact Journalism” last fall. Available online for free, it offers a selection of best practices in impact journalism, both in France and internationally.

While waiting for the English translation of the guide, GIJN reached out to two of the co-authors to learn more: Pierre Leibovici, deputy editor-in-chief for climate and pollution at Disclose and co-coordinator of impact strategy, and Timothée Vinchon, editor and co-founder of Rembobine.

title: The Power of ‘Positive Deviant’ Data Investigations: How Good Outliers Can Expose Systemic Misconduct or Policy Failure
content:
Investigative reporters often hear from a city or department official that “We just don’t have the budget” to solve some severe problem. Or, say, claims from a hospital administrator that their abnormally high rate of medical procedures is about clinical need or patient choice, rather than profiteering.

One effective approach for holding these actors accountable is with damning contrasts: by presenting their policies and outcomes side-by-side with comparable institutions that avoid those problems despite near-identical resources.

In Argentina, La Nación exposed the needless mass exclusion of children with disabilities from mainstream schools in most of the country by digging into the model of one province, La Pampa, where 98.5% of students with disabilities are enrolled in mainstream schools.

title: Using Archives in Investigative Reporting
content:
In this masterclass, Tristan Ahtone, editor-at-large at Grist and member of the Kiowa Tribe, shares practical techniques for using historical archives and colonial documents as accountability tools in investigative reporting.

Ahtone explains why historical context is essential when reporting on Indigenous communities, land, and institutions and how to use archival evidence to expose wealth transfer and institutional profit. He walks through key strategies: identifying relevant government records and archives, connecting historical documents with contemporary data, and building sources within institutions that interact with these systems.

title: NEW COURSE ADDED: AI Without the Guesswork: Smarter Journalism Without Prompting and Hallucinations
content:
Note: Curated courses are fee-based, allowing us to sustainably support our team and trainers while continuing to provide free, high-quality investigative journalism training opportunities worldwide. The training is live and there will be no recording.

Due to popular demand, GIJN has added a third, six-hour online masterclass for investigative journalists with Henk van Ess.

There is a built-in flaw affecting every AI conversation a journalist has and almost nobody is addressing it: writing an AI prompt does not involve asking it a neutral question. Instead, you are priming the tool to answer a certain way — through your word choice, your framing, and what you leave out. The tool takes in that request and returns it to you, tidied. You read the reply and feel informed. What actually happened is that you had a conversation with a cleaner, faster version of your own assumptions.

In this course, van Ess will explain why you should never ask a bot to “summarize this,” “give me bullet points,” or “what is the main point?”

title: Reporter’s Guide to Investigating Cryptocurrency
content:
Criminals and corrupt actors are using cryptocurrency to move money discreetly across borders, and largely bypass the traditional financial system. Crypto has also become a tool for businesses and wealthy individuals to funnel eye-popping amounts of money to politicians. At the same time, the crimes that crypto facilitates harm victims worldwide, causing hundreds of millions of dollars in losses per year in the United States alone, according to the FBI. All this has made investigating crypto transactions increasingly essential to accountability journalism. But the way this alternative financial system works can make that difficult.

At the core of crypto lies a paradox: while the technology can provide users with significant anonymity, it also permanently records most transactions on public ledgers known as blockchains. With the right investigative tools and techniques, these records can become a powerful source of reporting leads and revelations.

title: Spreadsheets for Investigative Journalists
content:
In this masterclass video, Helena Bengtsson, the data journalism editor at Gota Media and Bonnier News Local (two regional publishing companies in Sweden with 55 local titles), shares essential spreadsheet skills every journalist needs to tell impactful stories.

She explains how spreadsheets serve two core purposes in the newsroom: putting individual tips into context to produce better-reported stories and structuring information in a way that reveals the story itself.

Bengtsson walks through the five key techniques journalists should master: sorting to find the biggest numbers, filtering to isolate relevant data, performing simple calculations, building pivot tables to summarize large datasets and surface errors, and connecting multiple spreadsheets to compare data across sources. She also shows how combining two datasets (such as a list of politicians and a list of companies holding government contracts) can be a powerful method for detecting corruption.

title: How a WhatsApp Community Is Bringing India’s Data Storytellers Together
content:
A few years ago, when the COVID-19 pandemic had brought the world to a standstill, a small group of journalists, designers, researchers, developers, and civic technologists working with data in India started discussing an idea. They were not planning any online event. Mostly in isolation, they were simply trying to find one another.

In many of their newsrooms, universities, and companies, they were the only people doing data reporting or visualization. There was no common space where they could ask questions, exchange ideas, or meet others facing the same challenges. That conversation has now grown into one of India’s most active data storytelling communities.

Today, the VizChitra WhatsApp community has more than 1,600 members. Earlier this month, more than 600 people gathered both virtually and in real life — 400 of them attending in person from 55 cities across 20 states —  in the southern Indian city of Bengaluru for VizChitra 2026, a volunteer-led conference on data visualization and storytelling. The audience reflected the diversity of the community itself. Journalists sat alongside designers, developers, researchers, educators, product managers, students, and data scientists.

title: How StreetPress Became France’s Far-Right Investigations Engine
content:
In the run-up to France’s snap legislative elections in June 2024, the online news outlet StreetPress published a series of explosive investigations into far-right National Rally (RN) candidates. Uncovering racist statements, affiliations with extremist groups, and other controversies, the reporting ultimately prompted several candidates to withdraw from the race. The revelations became one of the biggest media stories of the campaign.

For a small, scrappy independent newsroom with an annual budget of €1.5 million (US$1.65 million) and a full-time staff of just 14 at the time (that number has since grown to 24), this was a significant coup. But over the past 16 years, the Paris-based outlet has quietly built a reputation for consistently punching above its weight, particularly in its uncompromising coverage of the French far right.

StreetPress was launched in 2010 by three journalists in their twenties, none of whom had studied journalism. Backed only by a €5,000 bank loan that co-founder Johan Weisz-Myara had secured under the pretext of renovating his apartment, it initially relied heavily on unpaid citizen journalists.
snippet: In the run-up to France’s snap legislative elections in June 2024, the online news outlet StreetPress published a series of explosive investigations into far-right National Rally (RN) candidates.
creator: Christopher Clark
